# Background {.unnumbered}

This assignment will guide you through the implementation of [PageRank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PageRank) using the numerical methods we've learned so far. Let's refresh our memory of the problem description:

Let $\mathbf{A} \in \{0,1\}^{n \times n}$ represent the connectivity matrix of $n$ web pages with entries

$$
a_{ij} = \begin{cases}
1, & \text{if page $i$ links to page $j$} \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Remember that $\mathbf{A}$ is not necessarily symmetric so we define $r_{i} = \sum_{j} a_{ij}$ as the *out-degree* of page $j$, reflecting the number of outgoing links from page $i$.
Imagine a random (web) surfer exploring the space of $n$ pages according to the following rules:

- From page $i$ with $r_{i} > 0$:
    - With probability $1-p$ they choose a link on a page $i$ uniformly at random and follow that link to the next page.
    - With probability $p$ they choose one page from the set of all $n$ pages uniformly at random and proceed to that page.
- From page $i$ with $r_{i} = 0$ (a dangling page), they randomly choose one page from the set of $n$ pages uniformly at random, thus avoiding getting stuck at a page without outgoing links.

We will refer to $p$ as the teleportation parameter, such that higher values correspond to the surfer following links and lower values allowing for more teleportation.
Put together, the description above defines a Markov chain governed by its [transition matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_matrix) $\mathbf{P}$.

According to standard Markov chain theory, the (random) position of the surfer converges to the stationary distribution $\mathbf{x} = (x_{1}, \ldots x_{n})^{\top}$ of the Markov chain.
Each component $x_{i}$ has the natural interpretation of the proportion of times the surfer visits page $i$ in the long run.
Therefore, $\mathbf{x}$ serves as a ranking of pages: a higher $x_{i}$ means page $i$ is visited often.
It is well-known that $\mathbf{x}^{\top}$ is the left eigenvector corresponding to the top eigenvalue 1 of the transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$.
That is,
$$
\mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}
\quad \text{or equivalently} \quad
\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}.
$$
This equation can be solved as an eigen-problem.
It can also be cast as solving a linear system of equations, namely $(\mathbf{I}_{n} - \mathbf{P}^{\top})\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ subject to the linear equality constraint $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} = 1$, ensuring $\mathbf{x}$ represents a probability vector.
We can view this as the extended system
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{I}_{n} - \mathbf{P}^{\top} \\
\mathbf{1}_{n}^{\top}
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{0}_{n} \\
1
\end{bmatrix},
$$
which has full column rank (the original system $\mathbf{I}_{n} - \mathbf{P}^{\top}$ is rank deficient due to the row-stochastic property $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{1}_{n} = \mathbf{1}_{n}$).
The insight we gain from this analysis is that, for an iterative solver, we can seed the initial guess with a vector with all positive entries to guarantee we recover a valid solution to the PageRank problem *without* directly enforcing $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} = 1$.
The [Perron-Frobenius Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem) guarantees existence and uniqueness here.

# Problem 2: Understanding the Transition Matirx $\mathbf{P}$ {#sec-prob2}

Let $X_{k} \in \{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ denote the page visited by the surfer after $k$ steps.
Let $Z$ denote the event that the surfer teleports (with probability $\Pr(Z) = p$), and $Z^{c}$ denote the event that the surfer follows a link (with probability $\Pr(Z^{c}) = 1-p$).

By the Law of Total Probability and the Markov property, the one-step transition probability from page $j$ to page $i$, which we represent with notation $P_{ij} = \Pr(X_{k+1}=i \mid X_{k} = j)$, is given by
$$
P_{ij} = \Pr(X_{k+1} = j \mid X_{k} = i, Z)\Pr(Z) + \Pr(X_{k+1} = j \mid X_{k}=i,Z^{c})\Pr(Z^{c}).
$$
These one-step probabilities only depend on the previous state, $X_{k} = i$.

Use the relation above to enumerate all possible entries $P_{ij}$ in terms of web page connectivities, $a_{ij}$, out-degrees $r_{j}$, total pages $n$, and teleportation parameter $p$.



# Problem 3: Identifying Structure in $\mathbf{P}$ {#sec-prob3}

The matrix $\mathbf{P}$ is dense, in fact it is completely filled in.
Yet, it can be described as a **sparse plus low-rank matrix**.
Using your answer from [Problem @sec-prob2], write down an expression for $\mathbf{P}$ as a sum of a sparse and a low-rank matrix.



# Problem 4: Fast Matrix-Vector Products {#sec-prob4}

We'd like to leverage the existing software like [KrylovKit](https://github.com/Jutho/KrylovKit.jl) to solve the PageRank problem.
Such tools expect us to provide a `Matrix`-like object for matrix-vector products.
Unfortunately, we cannot do this directly because $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_{n} - \mathbf{P}$ is dense.
To maximize performance, we need to exploit the structure of $\mathbf{P}$ by implementing fast matrix-vector products using a *wrapper type*.



## A. A Custom Matrix Type

The code below defines a type `PageRankPImP`, which consists of a connectivity matrix `A`, a teleportation parameter `p`, and a few additional arrays needed for the sparse + low rank representation.
Below it is a **constructor** that tells Julia how to build an instance of `PageRankImP` given a particular set of imputs.
Note that we *subtype* `AbstractMatrix{T}`, indicating that the object will behave like a `Matrix`.

Finish implementing the constructor code so that it produces a valid representation of $\mathbf{I}_{n} - \mathbf{P}$.

::: {#6 .cell execution_count=0}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
# a type for the matrix M = I - P in the PageRank problem
struct PageRankImP{TA <: Number, IA <: Integer, T <: AbstractFloat} <: AbstractMatrix{T}
  A :: SparseMatrixCSC{TA, IA}  # adjacency matrix
  p :: T                        # teleportation parameter
  r :: Vector{T}                # :)
  v :: Vector{T}                # :)
  tmp :: Vector{T}              # storage for any intermediates
end

# constructor: using only A and p
function PageRankImP(A::SparseMatrixCSC, p::T) where T <: AbstractFloat
  n = size(A, 1)
  r = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  v = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  tmp = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  # TODO: Fill r and v with appropriate values
  return PageRankImP(A, p, r, v, tmp)
end
```
:::





## B. Polymorphism in Julia

The object above is useless by itself. The next three lines of code define **methods** for *existing functions* in the language specific to our type.
These definitions give our object new behaviors; hence [polymorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymorphism_(computer_science)).

::: {#8 .cell execution_count=0}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
import Base: getindex, size
import LinearAlgebra: issymmetric, mul!

# matrix element access M[i, j]
Base.getindex(M::PageRankImP, i, j) = (i == j) - M.d[i] * M.A[i, j] - M.v[j]
LinearAlgebra.issymmetric(M::PageRankImP) = issymmetric(M.A)
Base.size(M::PageRankImP) = size(M.A)
```
:::



Create an instance of `PageRankImP` using the `SNAP/web-Google` data with `p = 0.15` and display the following:

- `M`
- `issymmetric(M)`
- `size(M)`

The purpose of `PageRankImP` is to implement the matrix-vector product $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})\mathbf{x}$ efficiently.
This is achieved by providing a `LinearAlgebra.mul!()` method *specialized to* our custom type, `PageRankImP`.
This `mul!()` function is used internally by packages like IterativeSolvers, or even by code like `A * v`.

# Problem 5: Iterative Solvers {#sec-prob5}

## A. Solving the linear system

[GMRES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_minimal_residual_method) solves linear systems without assuming symmetry or positive/negative definiteness.

::: {#20 .cell execution_count=0}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
# normalize in-degrees to be the start point
x0   = vec(sum(A, dims = 1)) .+ 1.0
x0 ./= sum(x0)

# right hand side
b = zeros(n)

# warm up (compilation)
linsolve(transpose(M), b, x0,
  issymmetric = false,
  isposdef = false,
  maxiter = 1)

# output is complex eigenvalue/eigenvector
(x_gmres, info), time_gmres, = @timed linsolve(transpose(M), b, x0, issymmetric = false, isposdef = false, maxiter = size(M, 2))
```
:::



You will lose points if the following statement throws an `AssertionError`.

::: {#22 .cell execution_count=0}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
@assert norm(x_gmres - xsol) < 1e-6
```
:::



::: {.callout-tip}
### Hint

:::

## B. Solving the eigenproblem

The [Arnoldi Method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnoldi_iteration) is an iterative method for solving eigenproblems.

::: {#24 .cell execution_count=0}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
# warm up (compilation)
eigsolve(transpose(M), x0, 1, :SR, issymmetric = false, maxiter = 1)

# output is complex eigenvalue/eigenvector
(vals, vecs, info), time_arnoldi, = @timed eigsolve(transpose(M), x0, 1, :SR, issymmetric = false, maxiter = size(M, 2))
```
:::



You will lose points if the following statement throws an `AssertionError`.

::: {#26 .cell execution_count=0}

``` {.julia .cell-code}
x_arnoldi = abs.(Real.(vecs[1]))
x_arnoldi ./= sum(x_arnoldi)
@assert norm(x_arnoldi - xsol) < 1e-6
```
:::
